clue.text: Spice up endless shanty

indicators.note: something without an end has lost its final part, so the closing letter is dropped

parts.note: a shanty is a song sung by sailors at sea

explanation.surface: An instruction to liven up a dull sailors' song by cutting its ending.
explanation.walkthrough: A shanty is a SEA SONG; lose its last letter and SEASON is left.
explanation.definitionFit: To season food is to add salt, herbs or spices, giving it more flavour.

clue.text: Start to observe twitching of the ear

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: first letter of observe
a tic is a nervous twitching of a muscle

explanation.surface: A doctor beginning to notice someone's ear twitching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twitching of the ear' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'of the ear'.
explanation.definitionFit: Otic is the medical adjective for anything relating to the ear, from the Greek word for ear.

clue.text: Prisoner accompanied by kind companion

parts.note: con is slang for a convict
a kind is a sort

explanation.surface: A convict who comes with a pleasant friend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' looks like an adjective describing the companion, but it is the noun meaning a type.
explanation.definitionFit: A consort is a partner or companion, especially the spouse of a reigning monarch.

clue.text: Man, perhaps Dennis, cycles after setter

indicators.note: to cycle is to go round, so the end letter moves round to the front

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as I
Les Dennis is a British comedian and game-show host

explanation.surface: A man, possibly called Dennis, riding his bike behind the puzzle's compiler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' looks like a person, but it is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea; Les Dennis is a British TV game-show host, and 'cycles' moves a letter of his first name round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man in the Irish Sea is one example of an island, so it is a definition by example.

clue.text: Test score's made when it goes ahead of 9

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an exam once taken by British children at about age eleven

definitions.text: score's made when it goes ahead of 9
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a sum that, followed by nine, totals twenty

explanation.surface: A cricket team's total reached once a batsman moves past nine.
explanation.walkthrough: A score is twenty, and eleven plus nine makes twenty, so 'it' is the answer read as arithmetic. The eleven-plus was a British exam deciding which secondary school a child attended.
explanation.definitionFit: The eleven-plus is the selective examination for grammar schools in parts of Britain, so it is a test.

clue.text: Chubbiness of lady's bottom with love bites spread over

indicators.note: letters spread over an area are scattered out of order
in a down clue the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: last letter of lady
love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheeky remark about love bites across a woman's ample rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' tempts as a body part, which suits the surface; here it picks out one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Chubbiness is plumpness, and obesity is the state of being very overweight, a stronger synonym.

clue.text: Indie band and boy band taking ecstasy with Queen

indicators.note: taking something away removes it, so one letter is taken out

parts.note: Blue were a British boy band of the 2000s
E is slang for the drug ecstasy
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: Two kinds of pop group, one taking drugs with a monarch or the rock band Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking ecstasy' suggests adding E, but here it means taking E away from BLUE.
explanation.definitionFit: Blur were a leading Britpop group of the 1990s, signed to an independent label, hence an indie outfit.

clue.text: "The Astronomer Royal will look into this" reported newspaper article

definitions.text: The Astronomer Royal will look into this

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by sound

parts.note: the i is a British national newspaper
a piece is a newspaper article

explanation.surface: A news report quoting the Astronomer Royal about something to be investigated.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look into this' sounds like investigating, but means literally peering into a lens. The i is a British newspaper; its name sounds like EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyepiece is the lens at the viewing end of a telescope, which an astronomer peers through.

clue.text: Old turtler, following excavation, discovered fins turned outward

indicators.note: with its covers taken off, a word loses its first and last letters

parts.note: ex means former

indicators.note: excavating hollows a thing out, leaving only its outer shell

parts.note: outside letters of turtler
dorsals are the fins on a fish's back

explanation.surface: A former turtle hunter finds fins after digging.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make it read as a story of digging, but excavation and discovery are both letter-stripping instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: Extrorsal is a botanical term for anthers that face or open away from the centre of the flower.

clue.text: List stuck on one side of my cooking pot

parts.note: a bill is a list, as of items owed or on a programme

indicators.note: a side of a word is one of its edges, here the right-hand end letter

parts.note: last letter of my

explanation.surface: A label or list stuck to the side of a cooking pot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One side of my' could be either end; only the last letter fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A billy or billycan is a metal tin used for boiling water or cooking over a campfire, especially in Australia.

clue.text: Help us to carry Calvin Klein footwear

indicators.note: carrying something means holding it within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: SOS is the distress call, read as save our souls
CK is the fashion brand's logo initials

explanation.surface: A plea for help carrying designer shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Help us' reads as an appeal, but it stands for the distress signal, whose letters are said to mean save our souls; the designer's initials go inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Socks are garments worn on the feet, and footwear covers anything worn there, so it is a broad category.

clue.text: Earwig goes lower, closer to small flies

indicators.note: a letter that flies away has left, so it is taken out

parts.note: goes means departs or leaves

indicators.note: the closer of a word is the letter that closes it, its last

parts.note: last letter of small
to lower something is to drop it

explanation.surface: An insect crawls downward, nearer to the tiny flies it hunts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earwig' looks like the insect but is the verb. 'Goes' gives LEAVES, which loses the last letter of 'small' to make EAVES.
explanation.definitionFit: To earwig is British slang for listening in secretly on other people's private conversations.

clue.text: Recoiling child with temperature given strange medicine

indicators.note: recoiling means springing back, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: a son is a child
T is the abbreviation for temperature
rum means odd or strange

explanation.surface: A feverish child flinching from an unusual remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange medicine' reads as one phrase, but 'strange' belongs to the wordplay as RUM.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostrum is a quack remedy, a medicine sold with exaggerated claims about its power.

clue.text: City break

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a port on the Croatian coast

explanation.walkthrough: 'City break' reads as a short holiday, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Split is the second city of Croatia, on the Adriatic, and to split something is to break it into parts.

clue.text: Miss preceded this well-bowled over by upcoming English player

parts.note: in cricket a maiden is an over in which no runs are scored off the bowler

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
a man is a player or piece in a game such as chess

explanation.surface: A tidy cricket over followed by a young English cricketer coming in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss' looks like a mistake, but it is the title of an unmarried woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's maiden name is her surname before marriage, the one that followed the title Miss.

clue.text: Salt judge put on egg

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another follows it

parts.note: a nit is the egg of a louse
to rate is to judge or assess

explanation.surface: A cooking instruction to season an egg with salt after tasting it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' looks like a verb in a recipe, but it is the noun, a chemical salt.
explanation.definitionFit: A nitrate is a chemical salt of nitric acid, such as saltpetre.

clue.text: Stagger through a complex network of paths

parts.note: taken as written
a maze is a confusing network of paths

explanation.surface: Someone lurching unsteadily through a labyrinth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stagger' reads as walking unsteadily, but it is meant as astonish.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagger someone is to astonish them, and amaze is a direct synonym for that sense.

clue.text: Tramp with a large rear end from Falkirk

parts.note: W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

indicators.note: the rear end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: last letter of Falkirk

explanation.surface: A big-bottomed vagrant from the Scottish town of Falkirk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' looks like a vagrant noun, but it is the verb for a long hike; 'rear' is a further distraction.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily or a long way on foot, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: "The beginning or the end for weak male?" scoffed colleague

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of weak
taken as written

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: last letter of weak
M is the abbreviation for male
to scoff is to eat greedily

explanation.surface: A colleague sneers at a feeble man, asking whether this is his start or finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoffed' reads as mocked, but it means gobbled. 'Weak' supplies both its first and last letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A workmate is someone you work alongside, which is what a colleague is, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Cantankerous ill youngster straddles potty

indicators.note: to straddle is to span across, so the letters lie across the word gaps

parts.note: letters running across the three words

explanation.surface: A grumpy sick toddler sitting astride a potty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' looks like a child's toilet, which fits the surface, but it is the adjective meaning crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Potty is informal British for mad or foolish, so it is a colloquial synonym of the answer.

clue.text: Happy chappies wiping backsides for fun

indicators.note: wiping off the backs of words removes their final letters

parts.note: gay in its older sense means happy
chappies are men

explanation.surface: Cheerful blokes wiping their bottoms just for a laugh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backsides' means the back ends of both words, so each loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A game is played for amusement, so something done as fun can be called a game, a loose synonym.

clue.text: Special gold and green piece of 25

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for special
Au is the chemical symbol for gold
sage is a grey-green colour

explanation.surface: A special gold-and-green section of something referred to elsewhere in the grid.
explanation.walkthrough: 25 is STRING; sausages come joined in a string, so one link is a piece of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Butchers sell sausages linked in a chain called a string, so each single link is part of that chain.

clue.text: Low-key performers removing the first of Band-aids

indicators.note: removing takes something out, so that letter goes

parts.note: bass players perform in a low register

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: first letter of Band

explanation.surface: Quiet musicians peeling off sticking plasters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Band-aids' reads as one word for plasters, but the hyphen splits it: 'Band' feeds the wordplay and 'aids' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To aid someone is to help them, and assists is the matching third-person verb form.

clue.text: Continuous striving for money and power beginning to rankle a bit

definitions.text: Continuous striving for money and power

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter

parts.note: first letter of rankle
taken as written
a trace is a small bit

explanation.surface: Endless ambition for wealth and influence starting to irritate somewhat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A bit' reads as 'somewhat', but 'a' and 'bit' give separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The rat race is the idiom for the competitive struggle of modern working life to get ahead.

clue.text: Nuns, accepting Jesus at last, resist going awry

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so one piece is held inside
going awry means going wrong, out of the proper order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: at the last means at the end, so the final letter is taken

parts.note: last letter of Jesus

explanation.surface: Nuns who take in Jesus finally, yet resist going astray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jesus' sits naturally beside nuns, but only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuns are addressed as Sister, so members of a religious order of women are called sisters.

clue.text: Series produced by pop star about the origin of reggaeton

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: Sting is the former lead singer of the Police

indicators.note: the origin of a word is where it begins, its first letter

parts.note: first letter of reggaeton

explanation.surface: A run of hits made by a pop singer on a new style of Latin music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Origin' sounds like the history of a genre, but it just picks one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A string of things is a series of them in a row, like a string of victories.

clue.text: Drunk seamen screening Ken Loach film are coherent

indicators.note: a screen surrounds and shields what is behind it, so one piece encloses another
drunk means reeling and confused, so the letters lurch out of order

parts.note: taken as written
Kes is Ken Loach's 1969 film about a boy and his kestrel

explanation.surface: Tipsy sailors watching a film manage to talk sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screening' suggests showing a film, which fits the surface, but it means enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that make sense are intelligible and logical, which is what coherent means.

clue.text: Use needles to inject young animal with nitrogen

indicators.note: an injection puts something inside, so one piece goes in the other

parts.note: a kit is a young fox, ferret or similar animal
N is the chemical symbol for nitrogen

explanation.surface: A vet using syringes to give a young animal nitrogen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Needles' and 'inject' suggest a syringe, but the needles are for wool.
explanation.definitionFit: Knitting is making fabric by looping yarn with a pair of long needles.

clue.text: Make the sound of a bird

indicators.note: a sound is something heard, so we go by pronunciation

parts.note: an erne is a sea eagle

explanation.surface: An instruction to imitate birdsong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make the sound of' reads as one verb phrase, but 'Make' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To make money is to earn it, so the verbs are synonyms in the sense of gaining income.

clue.text: Here in Quebec, undressed, we're colder

parts.note: ici is French for here, and Quebec is French-speaking

indicators.note: undressed means stripped of outer clothing, so only the inner letters remain

parts.note: middle letters of we're

explanation.surface: Canadians stripping off and finding it chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: Quebec is the French-speaking province of Canada, so 'here' becomes French.
explanation.definitionFit: Icy means very cold, so its comparative form matches colder.

clue.text: I'm on a social media platform that provides the bigger picture

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece on another sits above it, so it comes first

parts.note: taken as written without the apostrophe
taken as written
X is the platform formerly called Twitter

explanation.surface: Someone boasting that their social media account gives the full overview.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The bigger picture' sounds like an overview, but means a literally bigger cinema screen.
explanation.definitionFit: IMAX is a large-format film system with giant screens, so it literally shows a bigger image.

clue.text: Base removed from article in golf bag

indicators.note: removing one piece from another takes it out of that word

parts.note: the definite article
e is the base of natural logarithms
taken as written
Golf is G in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Removing the bottom of an item kept in a golf bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Golf bag' looks like one item, but 'bag' is the definition, used in its slang sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something is not my bag means it is not my thing, so the two are slang synonyms for a personal interest.

clue.text: Remember — two Finns were involved in this guy's plots

definitions.text: Finns were involved in this guy's plots

parts.note: to mark an occasion is to commemorate it
twain is an old word for two

explanation.surface: A reminder that a pair of Finnish people joined some scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finns' suggests people from Finland, but means Huckleberry Finn and his father, who appear in the novels.
explanation.definitionFit: The American novelist wrote The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, so characters named Finn were in his stories.
